title: Reading files: cat, less, head, tail, wc
lead: There is a right tool for every file: cat for small files, less for large ones; head for the start, tail for the end and live logs, wc for counting.
objectives: You choose the right tool by file size (cat, less, head, tail).
You read the start and end of a file with head and tail and the -n option.
You count lines, words and bytes with wc and do a small log analysis with grep -c and |.

sections.title: Choosing the right tool
body: On Linux, settings, logs and notes are mostly plain text files. There is no single command to read them; you choose by the **size and purpose** of the file.
Small file: `cat`. Large file: `less`. Start: `head`. End: `tail`. Follow live: `tail -f`. Estimate size: `wc`. Checking the size with `wc -l` first is a good habit.
sections.tip: When in doubt, run `wc -l notes.txt` for the line count first, then decide.

sections.title: Reading everything: cat and less
body: `cat` prints the whole file at once; fast and handy for short files. `cat -n` numbers the lines.

`less` opens the file page by page and does not flood the terminal. Inside: **Space** one page down, **b** one page up, `/word` searches, **q** quits. In the simulator `less` behaves like `cat`; try the real effect on your VM.

commands.why: The fastest way, but it cannot be paused.

commands.what: Prints the file with line numbers.
commands.where: When you talk about a line (error on line 7).
commands.why: Line numbers make discussion and debugging easier.

commands.what: Opens the file page by page; Space, b, /search, q.
commands.why: Does not fill the terminal, and you can search inside.

sections.warn: If you open a huge file with `cat`, the screen scrolls for minutes. Press `Ctrl+C` to stop it and use `less` next time.
sections.danger: Never print program (binary) files with `cat`: the terminal becomes garbled. Type `reset` to recover. If you are unsure it is text, look with `less`.

sections.title: Start and end: head and tail
body: `head` shows the first 10 lines, `tail` the last 10. Change the number with `-n`: `head -n 3 notes.txt`.

New log entries are added at the end, so `tail` shows the newest events. `tail -f` **follows** the file and prints new lines instantly; quit with `Ctrl+C`. With several files each one gets a header `==> name <==`.

commands.where: For header lines or the top of a configuration.
commands.why: A quick look into a big file.
Errors are usually at the end.

commands.what: Follows the file and prints new lines live.
commands.where: Watching the log of a running service.
commands.why: You catch the problem the moment it happens.

sections.tip: `tail -f` never ends on its own; it waits even if no new lines arrive. Quit with `Ctrl+C`.

sections.title: Counting: wc
body: `wc` (word count) gives lines, words and bytes. `-l` counts only lines, `-w` only words, `-c` only bytes. Without an option all three appear side by side: `3 6 33 notes.txt`.
Checking `wc -l` before opening a file prevents `cat` accidents.

commands.where: To learn the length of a log or list.
commands.why: A quick idea of the file size.
Measures the size of the content.

commands.what: Prints lines, words and bytes together.

sections.title: Combining: pipe and redirection
body: `|` (pipe) feeds the output of one command into the next: `head -n 6 app.log | tail -n 3` gives lines 4-6. `>` writes the output to a file instead of the screen.
`grep ERROR app.log` shows only lines containing ERROR; `grep -c` counts them. Details come in later modules; here we combine it with the reading tools.

commands.what: Selects the middle lines of a file.
commands.where: When you need a specific line range.
commands.why: Chaining both tools gives you a range.

commands.what: Counts lines that contain the pattern.
commands.where: When asking how many errors there are.

commands.what: Writes the output to a file.
commands.where: When keeping a result or attaching it to a ticket.

sections.warn: `>` erases the contents of the target file if it exists. Think twice before naming an existing file; use `>>` to append.
sections.danger: If you read and write the same file as in `cat notes.txt > notes.txt`, the file is emptied and the data is lost. Always redirect to a different file.

sections.title: Log paths by distribution
body: The main system log is `/var/log/syslog` on Debian/Ubuntu and `/var/log/messages` on RHEL/Rocky/Alma. A missing file gives `No such file or directory`; the problem is the path, not the command.
Many logs can only be read with `sudo` (for example `sudo less /var/log/secure`). Look first with `ls /var/log`.
sections.tip: If the file is missing, find the real name with `ls /var/log`. As a fallback `sudo journalctl -n 20` shows the latest entries.

t01.text: Read a small file with `cat notes.txt`.
t01.hint: The file is short, so cat fits.

t02.text: How many lines does `logs/app.log` have? Find out with `wc -l logs/app.log`.
t02.hint: The option is a lowercase L.

t03.text: Show the first 3 lines of the log with `head -n 3 logs/app.log`.

t04.text: Show the last 4 lines with `tail -n 4 logs/app.log`.
t04.hint: The last line should be 'shutdown complete'.

t05.text: Read the file with line numbers using `cat -n notes.txt`.

t06.text: Find the word count with `wc -w notes.txt`.
t06.hint: Three lines with two words each.

t07.text: See lines, words and bytes together with `wc Documents/report.txt`.
t07.hint: Without an option three numbers appear.

t08.text: Show the start of two files with one command: `head -n 2 Documents/list.csv Documents/report.txt`.
t08.hint: Each file gets a header `==> name <==`.

t09.text: Predict: what does `wc -l notes.txt` show? Run it and check.
t09.hint: Think of the line count you saw with `cat -n`.

t10.text: Predict: what happens with `cat logs`? Run it and read the error.
t10.hint: logs is a directory, not a file; expect 'Is a directory'.

t11.text: Predict: which line does `head -n 6 logs/app.log | tail -n 1` print? Run it and check.
t11.hint: The last of the first 6 lines, so line 6.

t12.text: Debug: a colleague typed `tail 5 logs/app.log` and got an error because `5` is treated as a file. Show the last 5 lines with the correct command.

t13.text: Mini project: write all errors to `errors.txt` with `grep ERROR logs/app.log > errors.txt`, then count them with `wc -l errors.txt`.
t13.hint: There should be three ERROR lines.

t14.text: Challenge: write only lines 4, 5 and 6 of `logs/app.log` to the file `middle.txt`.
t14.hint: Take the first 6 lines, then the last 3 of those, and redirect the result with `>`.

t15.text: Ticket: 'How many errors are on the server, and which are the first two?' Save the first two ERROR lines in `first_errors.txt` and show the total number of ERROR lines with `grep -c`.
t15.hint: `grep ERROR logs/app.log | head -n 2 > first_errors.txt`, then `grep -c ERROR logs/app.log`.

vm.intro: On your VM you only read; nothing is deleted. Reading system files is safe, but be careful not to overwrite files with redirection.

v01.title: Read a small file with cat
v01.text: Print the distribution information and paste the output.
differs: On Rocky/Alma you see `NAME="Rocky Linux"`; the fields may differ.
If you get `No such file` you may be in WSL or a container; try `cat /etc/hostname`.

v02.title: Read the start and end
v02.text: Show the first 5 and last 3 lines of the user file.
differs: The second line is `daemon` on Ubuntu and may be `bin` on RHEL.
The first line must always start with `root:x:0:0`.

v03.title: Count lines
v03.text: Find the line count of `/etc/passwd` and the three measures of `/etc/hostname`.
differs: Your line count depends on the installation; what matters is that a number and the file name appear.
In `wc /etc/hostname` the first number is lines, the second words, the third bytes.

v04.title: Browse with less
v04.text: Open the main log: `/var/log/syslog` on Ubuntu, `/var/log/messages` on RHEL/Rocky/Alma. Try Space, b, /error and q. When done press "Done".

blocks.cmd:
# Ubuntu
sudo less /var/log/syslog
# Rocky / Alma
sudo less /var/log/messages

differs: If the file is missing, look for its name with `ls /var/log`; some systems only have `sudo journalctl -n 50`.
If you cannot leave less, press `q`.

v05.title: Follow live (tail -f)
v05.text: Open two terminals. In the first follow the file; in the second append a line. When you see the new line, quit the first with `Ctrl+C` and paste the output.
differs: Terminal 1 stays empty and waits; that is normal until a line is appended.
With only one terminal do not pause `tail -f` with `Ctrl+Z`; open a second tab or window.

q1.q: Which tool is suitable for safely viewing a 5 GB log file?
options: less: shows it page by page
q1.explain: less shows only what fits the screen and lets you search; cat streams the whole file across the screen.

options: Follows the file and shows new lines live

q3.q: Which command gives only the number of lines in a file?

q4.explain: head shows the start; -n 3 means the first three lines. For the end use tail.

summary: Small file: `cat`; large file: `less` (Space, b, /search, q).
`head -n` shows the start, `tail -n` the end; `tail -f` follows live (quit with Ctrl+C).
`|` chains tools, `>` writes the result to a file; `>` overwrites existing files.
The log path depends on the distribution: syslog or messages.

glossary.meaning: A file where a program or system writes events in order.
A program that shows text page by page, such as less.
The | symbol; makes the output of one command the input of the next.
Writing output to a file instead of the screen; > or >>.
Watching the end of a file live with tail -f.
